about: Independent-reading plan for the 2026–27 school year. Core books are public domain and free to read online, download (EPUB/Kindle), or hear on LibriVox. One core book per module, matched to that module's ELA skill and history or science topic. Library picks are modern titles you can borrow free with a library card.

4.pace: About 20–30 minutes a day; read aloud together whenever a note suggests it.

books.title: Stories of King Arthur's Knights, Told to the Children
books.author: Mary Macgregor
books.why: Short, child-friendly retellings that run alongside the King Arthur unit in ELA, so independent reading reinforces class vocabulary.
books.ties: ELA Module 1 (King Arthur); word parts and context clues
prompts: Pick one unfamiliar word from today's chapter. What clues in the sentence helped you figure it out?
Which knight would you trust most? Give two details from the story.

books.title: A Child's Garden of Verses
books.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
books.why: A poem-a-week companion for the whole year: short, musical poems for reading aloud, copywork, and memorization.
books.ties: All modules: fluency, figurative language, copywork
prompts: Read the poem aloud twice. Which line has the strongest rhythm?
Copy your favorite stanza in your best handwriting and illustrate it.

books.title: Black Beauty (Young Folks' Edition)
books.author: Anna Sewell
books.why: A shortened edition of the classic told by the horse itself, ideal for practicing inference and theme in Module 2.
books.ties: ELA Module 2 (evidence, inference, theme); Science (animal needs and life cycles)
prompts: Black Beauty never says how he feels directly in this chapter. What can you infer, and what evidence shows it?
What lesson about kindness does the author want readers to learn?

books.title: Old Indian Legends
books.author: Zitkala-Ša
books.why: Dakota stories retold by a Dakota author, read alongside the Indigenous peoples of Mississippi unit. Pair with the Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians site already in the plan.
books.ties: Social Studies Module 3 (Indigenous peoples of Mississippi); ELA longer passages
prompts: How does Iktomi's trickery cause trouble? Track the evidence across two paragraphs.
Compare one legend with a Choctaw story or fact you learned this module.
books.note: Dakota (Sioux) legends from the Great Plains, not Mississippi nations; use them to compare oral traditions.

books.title: Winnie-the-Pooh
books.author: A. A. Milne
books.why: A gentle winter-break read-aloud with playful language; great for expression and fluency.
books.ties: Winter break read-aloud; ELA fluency
prompts: Read a Pooh conversation aloud with a partner using different voices.
Which character is most like you? Why?

books.title: Just So Stories
books.author: Rudyard Kipling
books.why: Invented words and silly 'how it came to be' tales make this a perfect match for interpreting words and phrases.
books.ties: ELA Module 4 (interpret words and phrases); Science (animal structures)
prompts: Find a made-up word Kipling uses. What do you think it means and why?
Write your own 'How the ___ Got Its ___' story in one page.

books.title: Peter Pan (Peter and Wendy)
books.author: J. M. Barrie
books.why: Pirates and adventure to read beside the adapted Treasure Island reader; compare how two authors build a villain.
books.ties: ELA Module 5 (Treasure Island; compare structure and viewpoint)
prompts: Compare Captain Hook with Long John Silver. Which is scarier, and why?
Who tells this story? How would it change if Wendy told it?
books.note: Contains outdated, stereotyped descriptions of Native characters (the 'Piccaninny' tribe chapters). Preview the chapters with that tribe (such as "The Happy Home") and talk about why the portrayal is hurtful.

books.title: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz
books.author: L. Frank Baum
books.why: Opens in Kansas with a cyclone, so it pairs with the Midwest region and the weather unit in the same module.
books.ties: Social Studies Module 6 (Midwest); Science Module 6 (weather)
prompts: How is Kansas described in Chapter 1? Compare it with what you learned about the Midwest.
What weather facts about tornadoes does the story get right or wrong?

books.title: Smoky the Cow Horse
books.author: Will James
books.why: 1927 Newbery Medal winner about a horse on a Western cattle ranch; supports the West/Southwest region study.
books.ties: Social Studies Module 7 (West/Southwest); ELA multiple texts
prompts: What ranch jobs does Smoky do? Connect them to the West's resources and economy.
How does Smoky change from the beginning of the book?
books.note: Written in cowboy dialect, so read the first chapters aloud together.

books.title: The House at Pooh Corner
books.author: A. A. Milne
books.why: Milne's Capitalized Important Words and playful punctuation make a fun springboard for the conventions module.
books.ties: ELA Module 8 (punctuation, capitalization, editing)
prompts: Find three words Milne capitalizes that normally would not be. Why do you think he did it?
Rewrite a short passage with standard capitalization. What changes?

books.title: West African Folk-Tales
books.author: W. H. Barker & Cecilia Sinclair
books.why: Short Anansi tales for summer reading and the final portfolio, ideal for retelling and presentations.
books.ties: ELA Module 9 (portfolio, presenting with evidence)
prompts: Retell your favorite Anansi tale to the family in under two minutes.
What lesson does the tale teach? Use one quote as evidence.
books.note: The introduction reflects 1917 colonial attitudes; start with the stories themselves.

library.title: The Tale of Despereaux
library.author: Kate DiCamillo
library.why: A tiny mouse who dreams of knights and chivalry; a perfect partner to the King Arthur unit.
library.access: Free with a library card (print, Libby or Hoopla)

library.title: Because of Winn-Dixie
library.author: Kate DiCamillo
library.why: A warm Southern small-town story; good for character and theme.
library.access: Free with a library card (print, Libby or Hoopla)

library.title: The One and Only Ivan
library.author: Katherine Applegate
library.why: Newbery winner told in short chapters by a gorilla; strong for inference and viewpoint.
library.access: Free with a library card (print, Libby or Hoopla)

library.title: The Wild Robot
library.author: Peter Brown
library.why: A robot learns to survive on an island; connects to life cycles and ecosystems.
library.access: Free with a library card (print, Libby or Hoopla)

library.title: Through My Eyes
library.author: Ruby Bridges
library.why: Ruby Bridges's own account of integrating her school; supports civics and the Southeast region.
library.access: Free with a library card (print, Libby or Hoopla)

library.title: Front Desk
library.author: Kelly Yang
library.why: An immigrant girl runs a motel front desk; great for comparing viewpoints and community.
library.access: Free with a library card (print, Libby or Hoopla)

library.title: Island of the Blue Dolphins
library.author: Scott O'Dell
library.why: Survival on an island off California; ties to the West region and natural resources.
library.access: Free with a library card (print, Libby or Hoopla)

7.pace: About 30–40 minutes a day, with a short written response each Friday.

books.title: The Call of the Wild
books.author: Jack London
books.why: A short survival novel about adaptation and environment that pairs with ecosystems and the theme work in Module 1.
books.ties: Science Module 1 (ecosystems); ELA central ideas and theme
prompts: How does Buck adapt to each new environment? Cite two moments.
State the theme in one sentence and support it with evidence.
books.note: Includes realistic animal violence and fighting.

books.title: Tales from Shakespeare
books.author: Charles & Mary Lamb
books.why: Prose retellings of Shakespeare's plays. Read 'The Tempest' before or alongside the class reader.
books.ties: ELA Module 1–2 (The Tempest)
prompts: Read the Lambs' Tempest. What details did they leave out of the play?
Which version helps you understand Prospero better, and why?

books.title: The Adventures of Tom Sawyer
books.author: Mark Twain
books.why: A Mississippi River classic with rich long passages for evidence and inference practice.
books.ties: ELA Module 2 (long-passage evidence and analysis); local connection to the Mississippi River
prompts: How does Twain use humor in the fence-whitewashing scene to reveal Tom's character?
Track one long passage: what is the central conflict, and how does it develop?
books.note: Uses period racial slurs and stereotypes (including of Injun Joe). Preview and discuss historical context before reading.

books.title: The Adventures of Odysseus and the Tale of Troy
books.author: Padraic Colum
books.why: A readable retelling of Homer for the Ancient Greece module.
books.ties: Social Studies Module 3 (Ancient Greece, mythology); ELA pronoun clarity in writing
prompts: Which Greek value (hospitality, cleverness, loyalty) does Odysseus show most? Give evidence.
How do the gods affect events? What does this tell you about Greek beliefs?

books.title: Julius Caesar
books.author: William Shakespeare
books.why: Shakespeare's play about the end of the Republic; Antony's funeral speech is a model text for purpose and viewpoint.
books.ties: Social Studies Module 4 (Republic vs. Empire); ELA purpose, viewpoint, and craft
prompts: Compare Brutus's and Antony's funeral speeches. Which persuasive techniques does each use?
Was Brutus a hero or a traitor? Argue with evidence from Act 3.
books.note: Read with a free audio version (LibriVox) or the Lambs' prose summary first.

books.title: The Arabian Nights Entertainments
books.author: Andrew Lang (ed.)
books.why: Selected tales (Aladdin, Ali Baba, Sindbad) for the Islamic Golden Age and trade modules.
books.ties: Social Studies Module 5 (Islamic Golden Age, trade); ELA modifiers in descriptive writing
prompts: What do the Sindbad voyages show about trade and travel in the Golden Age?
Highlight five vivid adjectives or adverbs in one tale and explain their effect.
books.note: Choose tales in advance; Lang's edition is family-friendly but long.

books.title: West African Folk-Tales
books.author: W. H. Barker & Cecilia Sinclair
books.why: Anansi and other oral tales from the region of the Ghana and Mali empires, for the West African kingdoms module.
books.ties: Social Studies Module 6 (West African kingdoms, trans-Saharan trade); ELA sentence structure
prompts: What role do storytellers (griots) play in preserving history? Compare with a written source.
Combine three short sentences from a tale into one precise sentence.
books.note: The introduction reflects 1917 colonial attitudes; pair with a modern source on Mali and Mansa Musa.

books.title: Otto of the Silver Hand
books.author: Howard Pyle
books.why: A short medieval novel about robber barons and a monastery childhood, matching feudalism and the medieval Church.
books.ties: Social Studies Module 7 (feudalism, medieval Church); ELA comparing sources and claims
prompts: Compare life in the castle and the monastery. What does each show about feudal society?
Is Pyle's picture of the Middle Ages accurate? Check two claims against your history reader.

books.title: The Weary Blues (selected poems)
books.author: Langston Hughes
books.why: Hughes's first collection, in the public domain since 2022, to read with the Harlem Renaissance ELA unit.
books.ties: ELA Module 7 (The Genius of the Harlem Renaissance)
prompts: Read 'Mother to Son' and 'Dream Variations.' How does Hughes use rhythm from blues and jazz?
Compare a Hughes poem with a reader passage about the same era.
books.note: Teacher-selected poems recommended; a few poems describe nightlife and cabarets.

books.title: The Trumpeter of Krakow
books.author: Eric P. Kelly
books.why: 1929 Newbery Medal winner set in 15th-century Kraków, with alchemy and early science, for the Renaissance and Scientific Revolution.
books.ties: Social Studies Module 8 (Renaissance, Scientific Revolution); ELA punctuation in dialogue
prompts: How does the alchemist Kreutz show the line between superstition and science?
Find a dialogue-heavy page and explain three punctuation choices.

books.title: Treasure Island
books.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
books.why: The original novel for the Age of Exploration module and summer reading.
books.ties: Social Studies Module 9 (Age of Exploration); ELA style, tone, and portfolio
prompts: How does Stevenson build suspense in the first five chapters?
Is Long John Silver a villain? Write a short argument for your portfolio.

library.title: Roll of Thunder, Hear My Cry
library.author: Mildred D. Taylor
library.why: Newbery winner set in Mississippi in 1933; essential Mississippi history through a family's eyes.
library.note: Depicts racism and racial violence; read and discuss together.
library.access: Free with a library card (print, Libby or Hoopla)

library.title: Hatchet
library.author: Gary Paulsen
library.why: Wilderness survival story to pair with The Call of the Wild.
library.access: Free with a library card (print, Libby or Hoopla)

library.title: A Single Shard
library.author: Linda Sue Park
library.why: Newbery winner set in 12th-century Korea; connects to medieval Asia and trade.
library.access: Free with a library card (print, Libby or Hoopla)

library.title: A Long Walk to Water
library.author: Linda Sue Park
library.why: Two Sudanese stories, past and present; supports African geography and Earth's resources.
library.access: Free with a library card (print, Libby or Hoopla)

library.title: The Inquisitor's Tale
library.author: Adam Gidwitz
library.why: Medieval France told by many narrators; perfect for feudalism and the medieval Church.
library.access: Free with a library card (print, Libby or Hoopla)

library.title: Brown Girl Dreaming
library.author: Jacqueline Woodson
library.why: A memoir in verse; pairs with Langston Hughes and the Harlem Renaissance unit.
library.access: Free with a library card (print, Libby or Hoopla)

library.title: Hidden Figures (Young Readers' Edition)
library.author: Margot Lee Shetterly
library.why: The Black women mathematicians behind NASA's space race; supports astronomy and space exploration.
library.access: Free with a library card (print, Libby or Hoopla)

platforms.title: CommonLit
platforms.what: Free leveled passages with questions and paired texts. Use it to add short readings to 'compare sources' weeks.

platforms.title: ReadWorks
platforms.what: Free nonfiction articles and 'Article-A-Day' science and social studies sets with audio.

platforms.title: StoryWeaver
platforms.what: Thousands of openly licensed illustrated stories in English and Spanish, by reading level.

platforms.title: Project Gutenberg
platforms.what: 70,000+ public-domain e-books in EPUB, Kindle, and web formats.

platforms.title: LibriVox
platforms.what: Free volunteer-read audiobooks of public-domain books, including most titles on this list.

platforms.title: Open Library
platforms.what: Borrow digital copies of modern books for free from the Internet Archive.

platforms.title: Mississippi History Now
platforms.what: Free Mississippi history articles and lesson plans from the Department of Archives and History.
